cards.title: Introduction to Spring Boot Configuration
cards.content:
Externalizing Configuration

Spring Boot allows you to externalize your configuration so that you can work with the same application code in different environments.

You can use application.properties or application.yml files located in your src/main/resources directory to define key-value pairs.

server.port=8080
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/mydb

options.text: YAML uses indentations to express hierarchical configuration data, whereas properties files use dotted keys.
Properties files support list structures natively, but YAML does not.
YAML files are converted to XML at runtime by Spring Boot.
Properties files allow duplicate keys without overriding previous values.

cards.title: Injecting Values with @Value
cards.content:
Using @Value Annotation

The @Value annotation is used to inject field values directly from properties files into Spring-managed beans.

@Component
public class GreetingService {

    @Value("${app.greeting:Hello World}")
    private String greetingMessage;

    public String getGreeting() {
        return greetingMessage;
    }
}

Syntax note: ${property.name:default_value} allows providing a fallback default value if the property is missing.

content.text: To inject the property 'server.timeout' with a default value of '5000', write the annotation as @Value("[[blank1]]").

cards.title: Type-Safe Configuration with @ConfigurationProperties
cards.content:
Type-Safe Configuration

For strongly typed, structured, and grouped properties, use @ConfigurationProperties instead of multiple @Value annotations.

@Component
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "mail")
public class MailProperties {
    private String host;
    private int port;
    private String username;
    // Getters and setters required
}

This automatically binds properties starting with mail.* (e.g., mail.host, mail.port) directly to fields.

pairs.right: Best for injecting individual scalar values
Best for binding complex hierarchical properties

cards.title: Environment Profiles in Spring Boot
cards.content:
Working with Spring Profiles

Spring Profiles provide a way to segregate parts of your application configuration and make it available only in certain environments.

File-based profile convention: application-{profile}.properties or application-{profile}.yml.

For example, application-dev.properties or application-prod.properties.

To activate a profile at startup:

java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

cards.title: Externalized Configuration Precedence
cards.content:
Property Source Precedence Order

Spring Boot uses a specific order designed to allow sensible overriding of values. Higher priority sources override lower priority ones.

  • 1. Command-line arguments
  • 2. Java System properties (System.getProperties())
  • 3. OS Environment variables
  • 4. Profile-specific application properties outside packaged jar
  • 5. Profile-specific application properties inside packaged jar
  • 6. Application properties outside packaged jar
  • 7. Application properties inside packaged jar
